nodes.title: Before the Big Bang?
nodes.subtitle: Why is there anything?
nodes.size: No size: maybe no space yet
summary: Nobody knows yet.
Maybe there was no "before".
details: ## What we can say
Our physics works back to a tiny fraction of a second after the start.
Before that, we have only ideas.
## Ideas people test
Inflation that runs forever, a bounce from an older universe, or time itself starting.
deeper: Why these laws? Why these numbers?
Chain Theory says only pairs of qudits exist. It does not say where they came from.
Gravity waves from the first instant (B-modes): best limit r < 0.034. The big US CMB-S4 was cancelled (2025); Simons Observatory and LiteBIRD (~2036) carry on.

nodes.size: Below all lengths (space is built later)
summary: A new idea by Alex Wissner-Gross (Oct 2026).
Reality = networks of linked tiny quantum units.
Brand new. Not yet tested by others.
details: ## Alex says
"Nothing exists but finitely many maximally entangled pairs of qudits, some qudits shared, known only by distilling them."
That one sentence is the only input. Alex aims for "no free parameters".
Particles would be "chainmail": finite meshes of these links. "A chain, not a string."
## Our reading
It is like a building made only of linked rings. Everything else is how the rings join.
deeper: A compendium of 100 theorems, 109 conditional theorems and 198 open results (release 0.1).
"Theorem" here often means a check over a finite list of networks, not a proof for all.
That its pieces ARE real physics is called a conjecture by Alex himself.
Peer review. Independent checks. A second number that matches a measurement.
Posted 23–24 Oct 2026. No independent expert review found yet (checked 6 Nov 2026).
Made with a "human-superintelligence collaboration". The author has a financial interest in Physical Superintelligence PBC.

nodes.title: Quantum fields
nodes.subtitle: Standard Model: tested
summary: Every particle is a ripple in a field.
The Standard Model: 17 particles, 3 forces.
Tested extremely precisely.
details: ## Recipe
12 matter fields (6 quarks, 6 leptons) + force fields (gluons, photon, W, Z) + the Higgs field.
## How it works
A field is spread over all space. A ripple of fixed size is a particle.
The rules come from symmetry: SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1).
deeper: Its predictions match experiments, e.g. the electron's magnetism to about 1 part in a trillion.
About 19–26 constants must be measured (masses, strengths). The theory does not explain them.
No gravity. No dark matter. Why 3 generations? Why these masses?

nodes.title: Quantum gravity
nodes.subtitle: Gravity at tiny scales?
summary: Joining gravity with quantum rules.
Ideas: strings, loops, chains…
None proven. No leading winner.
details: ## Why it matters
At the Planck scale (~10⁻³⁵ m) both gravity and quantum effects are strong.
Our two best theories then disagree.
## Candidates
String theory, loop quantum gravity, causal sets, "spacetime from entanglement", Chain Theory.
deeper: No idea is tested, and none leads by evidence.
Lab tests of "gravity-made entanglement" (tiny diamonds, atoms) are being designed; none done yet. LISA (2035) will listen to black holes merging.
Its gravity results are all graded "open" (Open result 1.9).

nodes.label: Chain Theory
nodes.label_note: Chain Theory is one candidate starting point, not established physics. Nothing established on this map depends on it.
nodes.subtitle: The links of the chain
summary: A qudit is a tiny quantum unit with d states.
Two qudits share one perfect entangled state.
That pair is one "link".
details: ## Alex says
A qudit has dimension 2 or more (2 = qubit, 3 = qutrit).
A pair is "maximally entangled": as linked as quantum rules allow.
A shared qudit is the end of 2+ pairs. It carries one copy per pair (because entanglement is "monogamous").
## Recipe
2 qudits → 1 link. Links join at shared qudits → a network.
deeper: A less-than-perfect pair would need smooth, continuous numbers. A fully discrete theory cannot have them.
Monogamy of entanglement and tensor networks (PEPS) are standard quantum information.
That reality is made ONLY of these pairs is the untested part.

nodes.title: Distillation
nodes.label: Chain Theory
nodes.label_note: Chain Theory is one candidate starting point, not established physics. Nothing established on this map depends on it.
nodes.subtitle: "To know is to link"
summary: To look at a link, you distill it.
Distilling 2 qudits makes them a new pair.
Time = a count of these acts.
details: ## Alex says
To distill two qudits is to project them onto a perfect pair. One copy, no failure.
A "read" is a distillation at one end of a pair.
What is "known" is only what reads can fix with certainty.
## Like
Entanglement swapping: link 1–2 and 3–4, distill 2 with 3, and now 1–4 is a pair.
deeper: "Time is counted, not assumed." Graded a conditional theorem (box 50.1).
The usual quantum probability rule comes out as an output (Alex grades it conditional).
Entanglement swapping is a real lab effect (since 1998).

nodes.title: Inflation
nodes.subtitle: Super-fast first stretch
nodes.size: Model-dependent: far smaller than a proton → roughly cm–m
summary: Space grew hugely in a split second.
Fits what we see in the sky.
Leading model, not proven.
details: ## How it works (model)
A field made space grow by a factor e (~2.7) again and again: at least ~60 times ("e-folds"), ~10²⁶ in all.
In common models it ended by ~10⁻³² s, then dumped its energy as hot particles.
## Why we think so
Space is flat, the sky is the same everywhere, and the seed ripples have the right pattern.
deeper: What field? Was it really inflation? No "B-mode" gravity-wave sign yet: r < 0.034.
Newest data (with DESI) lean away from the simplest (Starobinsky) model. Not settled.
Rivals: bouncing universes, other early phases.

nodes.subtitle: Only 2 can be read
summary: Links are typed by end sizes: (2,2), (3,2)…

The other four are "dark".
details: ## Alex says
Ends have dimension 2, 3 or 4 ("Conjecture 0", a conditional theorem).
A link is readable when d₁×d₂ ≤ 6 (math of Størmer, Woronowicz, Choi).
## Alex's conjectured jobs
(2,2) spacetime · (3,2) photon / electromagnetism · (4,2) weak force · (3,3) strong force · (4,3) Yukawa (mass) · (4,4) Higgs.
deeper: The 6 genres and the read cap are derived. Which physics each one IS: conjectured, some matched only "by name" (Alex’s words).
Bound entanglement (Horodecki 1998) first appears when d₁×d₂ > 6. That part is solid.

nodes.label: Chain Theory
nodes.label_note: Chain Theory is one candidate starting point, not established physics. Nothing established on this map depends on it.
nodes.subtitle: Qutrit + qubit symmetry
summary: A qutrit linked to a qubit has a symmetry.
It is the same shape as the Standard Model's.
A striking match. Meaning not yet proven.
details: ## Alex says
Turning the qutrit end gives SU(3). Turning the qubit end gives SU(2). One shared phase gives U(1).
Together: (SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1))/ℤ₆, the exact group of the Standard Model.
Its charge is the hypercharge with Y = 1/6, like the left-handed quark doublet.
deeper: The group S(U(3)×U(2)) ≅ (SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1))/ℤ₆ is known (Baez & Huerta 2010).
Alex's new step is reading it as the symmetry of ONE entangled pair.
Why this pair and not others? How hypercharge becomes electric charge is "beyond the Letter".

nodes.label: Chain Theory
nodes.label_note: Chain Theory is one candidate starting point, not established physics. Nothing established on this map depends on it.
nodes.subtitle: α is measured; this formula is new
summary: α sets how strongly light and charge interact.
Alex gets 1/137.035999190 with no tuning.
Measured: 1/137.035999177 (±21 in last digits).
details: ## Recipe (Alex says)
1 shared qutrit with 3 links to qubits, 2 of them read.
Count 172 "records": 79 + 48 + 42 + 3.
## Check
We re-did the sum: 1/α = 137.0359991896.
deeper: The number is proven from his rules, checked in Lean 4.
That it IS α is the "Photon Conjecture". It is not in the Lean proof.
0.6σ from CODATA 2022. But +1.6σ (electron g−2, 2023), −1.5σ (rubidium, 2020), +5.3σ (caesium, 2018). The experiments disagree with each other.
One blogger estimated ~140 formulas of this style land as close (rough, not peer-reviewed). No second matching number yet.
New, ~10× sharper measurements (Northwestern, Berkeley, Paris) will confirm or kill it.
His number sides with rubidium, against caesium. If caesium is right, it fails.

nodes.subtitle: Tiny bumps, 1 in 100,000
summary: Tiny quantum jitters were stretched huge.

Every galaxy grew from one.

That they came from inflation's quantum jitter is the leading idea, not proof.

nodes.title: Hot Big Bang
nodes.subtitle: Hot, dense, expanding
nodes.size: Today's visible universe was once tiny
summary: 13.8 billion years ago.
Hot, dense, and expanding ever since.
Seen in the afterglow light.
details: ## What it is
Not an explosion in space. Space itself stretching, everywhere.
## Timeline
10⁻¹² s: forces split. 10⁻⁵ s: protons form. 3 min: first nuclei. 380,000 yr: atoms.
deeper: Galaxies move apart (Hubble). The afterglow (CMB). The right amounts of H, He, Li.
The "Hubble tension": two ways of measuring the expansion speed disagree (~67 vs ~73 km/s/Mpc).

nodes.title: Higgs field
nodes.subtitle: Gives tiny particles mass
summary: Its particle was found in 2012.
It gives quarks, electrons, W and Z their mass.
NOT most of YOUR mass (see protons).
details: ## How it gives mass
Particles get mass by coupling to the field's steady value (246 GeV) everywhere in space.
## The numbers
Higgs boson: 125.2 GeV (PDG 2024). Found by ATLAS and CMS at CERN, 4 July 2012.
deeper: Only ~1% of a proton's mass comes from Higgs-given quark masses. ~99% is strong-force energy.
Why these couplings? Is the vacuum stable? Do neutrinos get mass this way? Unknown.
Alex conjectures the Higgs is a "closed hub read" in (4,4) links (conditional).

nodes.title: Chainmail particles
nodes.label: Chain Theory
nodes.label_note: Chain Theory is one candidate starting point, not established physics. Nothing established on this map depends on it.
nodes.subtitle: Particles as webs of links
summary: Each particle = a small web of links.
Its insides can't be pulled apart by collisions.
So it looks like a point. Alex's idea.
details: ## Alex says
Particles have no visible parts because their parts are "undistillable", not too small.
Example, the electron web: 9 sites and 10 links. A core triangle of three (3,3) links plus one "hub assembly" (links of types (4,2), (3,2), (4,3), (2,2)).
Muon and tau add more hubs to the same core (the tau is "the third hub on the triangle core"). Alex reads this as 3 generations (conditional 152.1).
## Recipe
Links + shared qudits → closed webs.
deeper: 17 particles drawn on 16 webs: 1 on a theorem, 11 conditional, 2 open, 3 not yet in the release.
"That a web is the named particle is a conjecture."
A neat idea: like knots in chainmail. No mass or charge of a real particle has been derived from a web yet (Thm 176.1).
Prediction: no 4th generation. Fits LEP's count of 3 light neutrinos.

nodes.subtitle: (2,2) links → spacetime
summary: Alex: space and time are not given.
They come from counting links and acts.
Conditional results. Not proven.
details: ## Alex says
The Lorentz group (special relativity) appears as the symmetries of a "Hermitian split" (conditional, box 54.1).
Spacetime has 1 time + 3 space directions: "one against three" (a theorem of the networks).
Gravity is "a statement about counting": a metric from the depth of a web, curvature as a graph Laplacian (conditional).
A cosmological term (dark energy?) at the "depth exponent" (conditional).
deeper: "Spacetime from entanglement" (Van Raamsdonk 2010) and gravity from thermodynamics (Jacobson 1995) are real research lines.
No measured gravity number (like G) is derived yet. Much of Part VI (metric, worldline, horizon) is conditional or open.
Alex grades "spacetime from (2,2) links" as an open conjecture, with all four gravity results open (Open result 1.9).

nodes.title: Hot particle soup
nodes.subtitle: All particles, ~10⁻¹² s
nodes.size: The whole universe was hotter than 10¹⁵ K
summary: Right after the Big Bang: pure energy.
Energy turned into particle pairs (E = mc²).
~10⁻¹² s: the Higgs switches on; forces split.
details: ## Recipe
Heat energy → pairs of particles + antiparticles, made and destroyed all the time.
At ~10⁻¹² s (~10¹⁵ K) the Higgs field takes its value: the weak and electric forces split, W, Z, quarks and electrons get mass.
## Randomness
Which particles pop out where is quantum chance.
deeper: The LHC recreates these energies (13.6 TeV ≈ 10¹³ eV per collision).

nodes.title: Quarks
nodes.subtitle: 6 flavours, 3 colours
summary: Up, down, strange, charm, bottom, top.
Never seen alone: always stuck together.
Protons and neutrons are made of them.
details: ## Family
3 generations × 2 = 6 flavours. Each has 3 "colour" charges.
Up: +⅔ charge, ~2.2 MeV. Down: −⅓, ~4.7 MeV. Top: 173 GeV (heaviest).
## Recipe
Mass from the Higgs field. Held by gluons.
deeper: Electron-scattering showed hard points inside protons (SLAC, 1968). Top quark found 1995.
Alex: quarks as "quark bodies" on star-shaped webs (conditional).
Why 3 generations? Why such different masses?

## Why it matters
Gluon energy makes up most of a proton's mass.
deeper: Alex: the strong coupling as a "gluon closed read" in (3,3) links (conditional).

details: ## Family

## Recipe
Mass from the Higgs field. No colour, so no strong force.
deeper: Alex draws an electron web; muon and tau add hubs (conditional theorem 152.1). That the web IS the electron: conjecture.
Why is the muon 207× heavier than the electron? Unknown.

nodes.title: All 118 elements
nodes.subtitle: Tap for the table
summary: 94 found in nature, 24 only made in labs.

Tap "Open the periodic table".
details: ## Recipe
Element = Z protons + some neutrons + Z electrons.
Where they come from:
Big Bang: H, He, (Li). Big stars: O to Fe. Dying giants: about half past Fe. Neutron-star crashes: gold, uranium. White dwarfs: most iron.
## The abundance zig-zag

Oddo–Harkins rule: even-proton nuclei are usually more abundant than their odd-proton neighbours. Neutron–proton pairing makes even nuclei more tightly bound and stable, so nuclear physics, not chance, gives this pattern.
deeper: By mass the Sun is ~73% H, ~25% He, ~2% everything else.
Most superheavy elements (104–118) last seconds or less; the longest-lived (dubnium-268) ~16–30 hours (measurements differ).

nodes.title: String theory
nodes.subtitle: Rival: tiny vibrating strings
nodes.size: Strings near the Planck length (~10⁻³⁵ m)
summary: Particles = vibrating strings.
Needs extra hidden dimensions.
Rich maths, no test yet.
details: ## The idea
Every particle is one tiny string vibrating in a different way. Gravity comes out automatically.
It needs 10 dimensions (11 in M-theory); the extra ones would be curled up too small to see.
## Where it stands
The biggest quantum-gravity programme. It gave holography (AdS/CFT), a key tool. But it allows a huge number of possible universes, so it has not picked out ours.
deeper: No experiment has seen strings, extra dimensions or supersymmetry (LHC so far).
Strings start from objects in space; Chain Theory starts from links with no space at all.

nodes.title: Loop quantum gravity
nodes.subtitle: Rival: space made of loops
nodes.size: Smallest areas near the Planck scale
summary: Space itself comes in tiny chunks.
No extra dimensions needed.
No test yet.
details: ## The idea
Quantise space itself: areas and volumes come in smallest units, woven from loops (spin networks).
It needs no extra dimensions and no strings.
## Where it stands
A smaller programme than strings. Hard part: showing the smooth space we see comes back at large scales.
deeper: No measured effect yet. Some versions predict a "bounce" instead of a Big Bang start.
Closest in spirit: both build space from a network. Loops carry geometry; Chain Theory's links carry entanglement.

maths.title: Counting & number
maths.subtitle: Names for how many
summary: Numbers describe size, order and position. Different societies built different symbols and counting systems.
details: What counts as known: A definition or theorem is known mathematics only with explicit assumptions and a valid proof. Checking many examples is not a proof for every case.
Where it began: Counting and measurement developed across many cultures; there is no single inventor of "numbers".

maths.title: Place-value notation
maths.subtitle: Position carries value
summary: The value of a digit depends on its position. This makes large numbers and efficient calculation much easier.
details: Examples: Babylonian mathematics used base 60; decimal place value with zero developed in India and travelled through other mathematical traditions.
Careful credit: Place-value systems arose independently in more than one place; the story is not one straight chain of invention.

maths.title: Fractions & ratio
maths.subtitle: Parts of a whole
summary: A rational number is a ratio of two integers, with a nonzero denominator. Ratios compare quantities without needing a whole unit.
details: Equivalent forms: 2/3 and 4/6 name the same rational number. A fraction is a number, not a command to divide a physical object.
Beyond fractions: Numbers such as √2 cannot be written as a ratio of integers; the Greeks studied this tension geometrically.

virtual_cell.title: Typical human cell (generalised)
summary: A general human body cell, about 20 µm across: it has the parts most human cells share.
No single real cell type looks exactly like this; the shape is simplified.
details: Real human cells range from about 7 µm (red blood cells) to over 100 µm, and from round to long and branched.
Sizes and speeds of the parts inside are real measured values, drawn to scale.
Some counts are reduced so you can see between things: proteins at ~1/8 of real crowding, 30 of ~10,000 vaults, fewer microtubules and ribosomes.

virtual_cell.title: Cell membrane
summary: A skin of fat molecules two layers thick, about 5 nm.
It lets some things in and keeps others out.
details: Made of roughly a billion lipid molecules, with proteins floating in it.
In cells that crawl, the front edge ruffles and moves forward a few µm per minute (a lamellipodium).
Zoom right in to see the two layers of lipids.

virtual_cell.title: Chromatin (DNA)
summary: DNA wound on protein spools (nucleosomes).
Each spool holds 147 DNA letters, wrapped almost twice.
details: A nucleosome is about 11 nm wide and made of 8 histone proteins.

In living cells the beads fold into irregular chains 5–24 nm wide, not a neat uniform 30 nm fibre.

summary: A spool of 8 histone proteins with DNA wrapped around it.

mRNA goes out, proteins come in.

summary: A protein-building machine, about 25–30 nm.

details: A human cell has millions (estimates around 10 million in fast-growing cells).
Two parts: a small (40S) and a large (60S) subunit.

summary: A small bubble (50–100 nm) carrying cargo.

Off the track, a vesicle only jiggles slowly: the cytoplasm is very crowded.

L.name: Dying low-mass stars
L.note: Giant stars (1–8 Suns) catch neutrons slowly (s-process), then puff off their outer layers. (Most of our lithium: such stars and novae.)

M.name: Massive stars & their supernovae
M.note: Made by fusion, neutron capture and explosive burning in stars >8 Suns; spread by core-collapse supernovae. Includes most Cu and the simpler main-source choice for Zn, Ti and V; shares vary by isotope and remain debated.

W.name: Exploding white dwarfs
W.note: Type Ia supernovae: lots of iron-group metals.

N.name: Merging neutron stars
N.note: Rapid neutron catching (r-process). Maybe also rare supernovae (debated).

R.name: Radioactive decay only
R.note: No long-lived form; made as other elements decay.

H.name: Human-made
H.note: Made in reactors or accelerators (some also in traces or in stars, briefly).

not_yet_made.title: Ununennium (temporary name)
not_yet_made.summary: Not made yet. Hunts running: Dubna (JINR) began Bk-249 + Ti-50 on 1 June 2026, for several months. RIKEN (V-51 + Cm-248) paused after reaching its planned sensitivity, with no atom reported, and is planning its next step.

sources.title: JINR 2026: Dubna starts its element-119 experiment (Bk-249 + Ti-50)
RIKEN (TASCA26 abstract): the V-51 + Cm-248 search for element 119

not_yet_made.title: Unbinilium (temporary name)
not_yet_made.summary: Not made yet. Berkeley showed a Ti-50 beam can make superheavies (2 livermorium atoms in 22 days, 2024); 120 is expected to be 10–20× harder and could take years. ORNL is making a Cf-249 target (2026). An older GSI search (2011) saw one possible chain, never confirmed.

automatic_checks.what: Structural checks run by a script on every build (src/audit.py, report in AUDIT-v0.8.md): every card has a colour and at least one source, links point at cards that exist, share links are exact, the data hash is the same in every file, counts match, and every source URL was fetched to see that it answers.
automatic_checks.not: They do not read the science. Passing them does not mean a claim is right, only that it is labelled, sourced and linked.

science_review.what: A science review means a person with the right expertise reads each claim against its sources and decides whether it is right, up to date and fairly coloured.
science_review.how_to_help: Every card has a Suggest a fix button (e-mail). Please check claims against the listed sources and say what looks wrong.

stops.title: Our sky: the Milky Way from inside
stops.subtitle: Gaia's map of 1.7 billion stars
stops.shown_as: all-sky map on a ball around you
summary: We live inside the Milky Way, about 27,000 light-years from its centre, so we see it as a bright band across the sky. ESA's Gaia mapped about 1.7 billion of its stars.
details: What the picture is: Gaia's all-sky map (Data Release 2), built from star measurements, wrapped on a ball around you. Look around: the bright band is the disc of our galaxy, and the two smudges lower right are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.
Be careful: A sky map shows directions, not distances: stars on it are at very different distances.
Where we are: The Galactic Centre is 8.178 kiloparsecs away (about 26,700 light-years), measured by the GRAVITY Collaboration in 2019.

stops.title: A spiral galaxy like ours (M101)
stops.subtitle: the Pinwheel Galaxy, 25 million light-years away
summary: No camera has ever left the Milky Way, so nobody has a photo of our galaxy from outside. M101, the Pinwheel Galaxy, is a real spiral galaxy seen face-on by Hubble.
details: What the picture is: Hubble's largest galaxy portrait: 51 exposures plus ground-based images (ESA/Hubble, 2006). The photo is flat; real galaxy discs are thin but not flat paper.
Size and distance: About 170,000 light-years across, nearly twice the Milky Way, and about 25 million light-years away (ESA/Hubble).
Honest note: Our galaxy is a barred spiral; M101 is used here only as a real example of what a spiral galaxy looks like.

stops.subtitle: thousands of galaxies in a grain-of-sand patch of sky

stops.title: The oldest light: the cosmic microwave background
stops.subtitle: ESA Planck's map of the whole sky
stops.shown_as: all-sky map on a ball around us
stops.size: the edge of what we can see
summary: The farthest thing we can see is light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. ESA's Planck mapped it across the whole sky.
details: What the picture is: Planck's all-sky map of tiny temperature differences in the cosmic microwave background, wrapped on a ball with us at the centre. Microwaves are invisible, so the colours are false colours.
How far: Because space has expanded, the matter that sent this light is now about 46 billion light-years away: roughly the radius of the observable universe.
Honest note: It is a sphere around us because we see out in every direction; it is not a wall at the edge of the universe.

nodes.title: Newton's law of universal gravitation
nodes.subtitle: every mass pulls every other mass

Limits: It is an excellent approximation; general relativity replaces it for strong gravity and high precision.

nodes.title: Noether's theorem
nodes.subtitle: symmetry gives conservation laws
summary: Every continuous symmetry of the laws of physics gives a conserved quantity.
Same laws at every time → energy is conserved; at every place → momentum.
details: Proved: Emmy Noether proved it in 1918 (English translation 1971).
Everywhere: Rotation symmetry gives conservation of angular momentum; the symmetries of the Standard Model give conserved charges.

nodes.title: Elements of life (CHNOPS)
nodes.subtitle: six elements build most of life
summary: Most of the mass of every living thing is just six elements: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur.
Carbon can make four bonds, so it builds the chains and rings of life's molecules.
details: Carbon: Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds, giving a huge variety of molecule shapes.
Made in stars: Hydrogen comes mostly from the Big Bang; the other five were made in stars.

nodes.title: Biological macromolecules
nodes.subtitle: proteins, nucleic acids, sugars, lipids
summary: Four big families of molecules build every cell: proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids.
Most are long chains made by linking small units together.
details: Units: Amino acids → proteins; nucleotides → DNA and RNA; sugars → starch and cellulose.
Lipids: Fats and phospholipids are not long repeating chains, but they build membranes and store energy.

The cell is the basic unit of life, and every cell comes from an earlier cell.
details: Built: Schleiden and Schwann (1838–39) and Virchow (1855), after the first microscopes of Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek.
Viruses: Viruses are not cells; whether they count as alive is debated.

nodes.title: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
nodes.subtitle: without and with a nucleus
summary: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi, protists) keep their DNA in a nucleus and have organelles.
details: Size: Most prokaryotic cells are about 0.1–5 µm across; eukaryotic cells are usually about 10–100 µm.
You: Your body is built from eukaryotic cells, and carries many prokaryotes too.

nodes.subtitle: a fluid mosaic of lipids and proteins

It lets some things through and keeps others out.
details: Model: The fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): proteins float in a fluid layer of lipids.
Thin: About 5–10 nm thick.

nodes.title: DNA double helix
nodes.subtitle: the molecule of heredity
summary: DNA is two strands wound into a double helix, joined by base pairs: A with T, G with C.
The order of the bases stores genetic information.
details: Discovered: Watson and Crick proposed the structure in 1953, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling.
Size: One set of human chromosomes holds about 3 billion base pairs.

nodes.title: Central dogma of molecular biology
nodes.subtitle: DNA → RNA → protein
summary: Genetic information flows from DNA to RNA (transcription) and from RNA to protein (translation).
It does not flow back from protein to DNA or RNA.
details: Stated: Francis Crick, 1958; restated in Nature in 1970.
RNA → DNA: Retroviruses copy RNA back into DNA; this fits Crick's rule, which only forbids protein → nucleic acid.

nodes.title: Genetic code
nodes.subtitle: three letters for each amino acid
summary: Each three-letter codon in RNA stands for one amino acid, or "stop".
64 codons code for 20 standard amino acids, and almost all life uses the same code.
details: Cracked: Nirenberg and Matthaei read the first codon (UUU = phenylalanine) in 1961.
Shared: The near-universal code is strong evidence that all life shares an ancestor.

nodes.subtitle: catalysts that speed up life

Each one fits its target molecule at an active site.

RNA too: Some RNA molecules (ribozymes) are catalysts as well, including the core of the ribosome.

nodes.subtitle: the cell's energy currency

Splitting off its last phosphate releases energy that powers work, from muscles to building proteins.
details: Recycled: Cells remake ATP from ADP and phosphate again and again, mostly with the enzyme ATP synthase.
Parts: Adenine, the sugar ribose and three phosphate groups.

nodes.subtitle: mitosis copies, meiosis mixes
summary: In mitosis one cell becomes two identical cells, for growth and repair.
Meiosis makes egg and sperm cells with half the chromosomes, and shuffles the genes.
details: First: Before dividing, a cell copies all of its DNA.
Bacteria: Prokaryotes divide more simply, by binary fission.

nodes.subtitle: how chemistry became biology
summary: How non-living chemistry first became living cells is unknown.
Experiments show life's building blocks can form naturally, but no one has made life from scratch.

When: Life was present by about 3.5 billion years ago; how it began is still open.

Ribozymes show that RNA can do both jobs.

Status: Widely supported but not proven; how the first RNA formed is unknown.

They still have their own DNA and divide like bacteria.

nodes.subtitle: genes come in pairs
summary: Traits are passed on by separate units (genes), one copy from each parent.
Gregor Mendel found the rules by breeding pea plants.
details: Published: Mendel, 1866; rediscovered in 1900.
Laws: Segregation: the two copies separate into different sex cells. Independent assortment: different genes are often inherited separately.

nodes.title: Natural selection
nodes.subtitle: variation + inheritance → adaptation
summary: Individuals vary; variations that help them survive and reproduce are passed on more often.
Over many generations this adapts populations to their surroundings.
details: Published: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, 1858; Darwin's On the Origin of Species, 1859.
Seen today: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria evolves by natural selection.

Evolution became a change in how common gene variants are in a population.

Since: Molecular biology and genomics have extended it.

Often a barrier, such as a mountain range or a sea, separates them first.
details: Kinds: Allopatric (split by geography) and sympatric (in the same place).
Result: Over billions of years, speciation built the tree of life.
